extracted.intended_audience: math educators, researchers, and instructors evaluating mathematical problem solving
extracted.subtask_description: A rubric for analyzing the process quality of mathematical solution attempts using Schoenfeld's four-component framework (cognitive resources, heuristics, control/metacognition, beliefs) plus episode-structure coding and expert/novice process markers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cognitive Resources
rubrics_metrics.description: The propositional and procedural knowledge available to the solver (what the solver knows and can do).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the solver demonstrates relevant theorems, standard techniques, mental images of typical objects, or a repertoire of worked examples; judge adequacy relative to the demands of the problem (e.g., does the solver have the required background to make progress?). Examples listed: theorems known, standard techniques mastered, mental images, worked-example repertoire. A solution showing inadequate resources may flounder or misuse procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heuristics
rubrics_metrics.description: The strategies the solver uses to make progress when stuck, including both general and domain-specific heuristics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether heuristics are appropriate and productive (Polya-style heuristics such as working backward, drawing figures, looking for analogies; domain-specific heuristics such as trying small cases, exploiting symmetries, varying constraints; and general heuristics like simplifying or generalizing the problem). Flag random or inappropriate heuristic use as a weakness; prefer purposeful selection and sequencing of heuristics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control (Metacognition)
rubrics_metrics.description: The solver's monitoring and regulation of their own problem-solving: when and how they deploy resources and heuristics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for evidence of decisions such as when to use particular tools, when to abandon a fruitless approach, how time is allocated across subproblems, and when to back off and reconsider. Strong control includes verification of intermediate results and strategic allocation of effort; poor control includes persistence with failing approaches and failure to switch strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Belief Systems
rubrics_metrics.description: The solver's implicit and explicit beliefs about the nature of mathematics and problem solving, which shape choices and persistence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify productive beliefs (e.g., multiple approaches can exist, hard problems require restructuring, verification is part of solving, switching is sometimes necessary) versus counterproductive beliefs (e.g., 'math is mysterious', 'there's one right way', 'if I haven't seen this I can't solve it', 'problems should take <5 minutes'). Use these markers to explain why certain process behaviors occur and to evaluate long-term problem-solving capacity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Episode Structure (Read → Analyze → Explore → Plan → Implement → Verify)
rubrics_metrics.description: Coding which problem-solving episodes occur and their order: Read, Analyze, Explore, Plan, Implement, Verify.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Score solutions for presence/absence and sequencing of episodes. Expert-like solutions tend to include Analyze and Plan before heavy computation and loop back to Analyze when implementation fails. Novice-like solutions often jump from Read straight to Implement and skip Analyze/Plan. Recovery behavior (returning to Analyze after failed implementation) is a positive marker. Use episode presence and ordering as process-evaluation signals independent of final correctness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expert vs. Novice Process Markers
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirical differences identified between expert and novice problem solvers in protocol analyses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge whether the solution shows expert-like patterns: spending more time on analysis before computing; frequent verification of intermediate answers; strategic allocation of time across subproblems; flexible strategy switching. Conversely, mark novice-like patterns: over-reliance on familiar procedures without checking applicability; failure to switch strategies when an approach is failing; rushing to computation without analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implied Solution-Quality Criteria (summary)
rubrics_metrics.description: Schoenfeld's explicit statement of what makes a high-quality mathematical solution in process terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A high-quality solution shows adequate cognitive resources, use of appropriate heuristics (not random trial), strong control behaviors (analysis time, abandoning failing approaches, verification), productive beliefs, a healthy episode structure (Analyze and Plan present), and recovery behavior when approaches fail. Use these as scoring axes when evaluating solution processes, noting that they are process measures separate from correctness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poor-Process Markers (anti-patterns)
rubrics_metrics.description: Explicitly listed process features that indicate poor-quality problem solving.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Flag solutions that jump from Read to Implement, persist in failing approaches without abandoning them, contain no verification step, exhibit beliefs of mathematics-as-memory rather than reasoning, or apply heuristics inappropriately or randomly. Use these markers to diagnose why a solution succeeded or failed and to guide remediation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Belief-Specific Indicators (helpful vs. harmful beliefs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Concrete belief statements that help or hurt problem-solving capacity, usable as diagnostic markers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the provided examples to detect solver mindset: harmful beliefs include 'There is one right way', 'If I haven't seen this type before, I can't solve it', 'Math problems should be solvable in 5 minutes', and 'Long calculations mean you're doing it wrong'; helpful beliefs include 'Multiple approaches usually exist', 'Hard problems require restructuring', 'Verification is part of solving', and 'Switching away from a wrong approach is productive.' These indicators inform both evaluation and instructional intervention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adaptation to Research Mathematics
rubrics_metrics.description: How Schoenfeld's school-mathematics-focused framework transfers to evaluation of research-level mathematical work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating research papers or advanced solutions, check analogous markers: are the resources (relevant theorems, background) adequate; are heuristics and strategies well-chosen and justified; does the author show control by explicitly noting failed approaches and why they were abandoned; and do the author's beliefs about the area (e.g., preference for structural vs computational approaches) transparently shape the work. Use these as process-quality criteria for research outputs.
